key_messages: Scattered showers and thunderstorms are expected this afternoon, mainly across the Adirondacks, featuring occasional heavy downpours.

More widespread showers and thunderstorms are expected Tuesday through Thursday as a slow moving system tracks through the region through the midweek, bringing the potential for localized flash flooding.
An unsettled weather pattern prevails late week into next weekend as departing system is replaced by another developing mid/upper level trof.

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 243 AM EDT Monday...

Confidence has increased in the potential for heavier downpours
and localized flash flooding on both Tuesday and Wednesday. Area
of highest concern is northern New York, but any spot that sees
multiple days of heavy rain will need to be monitored.

Based on latest model trends, have incorporated a sharper 
gradient of precipitation chances and amounts Tuesday and 
Wednesday due to the main axis of moisture and instability over 
New York on Tuesday as well as southeasterly and easterly 
downsloping on Wednesday.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 243 AM EDT Monday...

1. Scattered showers and thunderstorms are expected this 
afternoon, mainly across the Adirondacks, featuring occasional 
heavy downpours.

2. More widespread showers and thunderstorms are expected 
Tuesday through Thursday as a slow moving system tracks through 
the region through the midweek, bringing the potential for
localized flash flooding.

3. An unsettled weather pattern prevails late week into next 
weekend as departing system is replaced by another developing 
mid/upper level trof.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 243 AM EDT Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Surface high pressure is currently stationed across the 
Ohio Valley early this morning with upper level troughing directly 
overhead northern New York and Vermont. Throughout the night, 
temperatures are expected to fall into the mid 50s to mid 60s. This 
will also bring the potential for patchy valley fog, especially in 
Adirondack locations that received rainfall yesterday (portions of 
western Adacks reported 0.50-1.50 inches). Throughout the day 
today, troughing will slide east of the region, but we should 
have enough shortwave energy, moisture, and warmth to allow for 
some showers and thunderstorms, about 25-65% chance in northern 
New York, highest in the northern Adirondacks. For Vermont, 
chances are lower in general, around 5-40%, and mainly in the 
Greens or from any precip that forms in the Adirondacks and 
holds together as it drifts eastward. Should the New York 
locations that received sufficient rainfall yesterday (these 
areas may include Hogansburg, Brasher, Tupper Lake, Parishville,
Horseshoe Lake, South Bombay, Stark, and eastern Potsdam) 
receive another round or two of showers or thunderstorms today 
we'll need to monitor these areas for potential flash flooding, 
but this threat is highly conditional. The Weather Prediction 
Center currently has most of northern New York, outside of the 
Champlain Valley, under a Marginal Risk (Risk level 1 out of 4; 
5% chance for rainfall exceeding flash flood guidance) for 
today. Northern New York rivers could see some small rises, but 
nothing near bankfull with the recent dryness we have had. 
Temperatures today will be in the upper 70s to mid 80s, slightly
above seasonal normals. Tonight, shower activity should dwindle
again like yesterday, and lows will be relatively mild in the 
mid 50s to mid 60s. Total precipitation amounts will be around 
0.10-0.25" in the Adirondacks and parts of the Greens, locally 
higher in heavy, slow moving storms.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A slow moving upper low is expected to track through the 
region midweek, bringing chances of persistent showery weather 
Tuesday through Thursday. On Tuesday, models place the upper low 
somewhere from the southern Ontario-Quebec line to central New York, 
and its associated surface low pressure around eastern Lake Ontario 
and central New York. This multi-layer low pressure is expected to 
move very little Tuesday and Tuesday night, spinning cyclonically 
over the Northeast and drifting slightly eastward. As it does so, it 
will send plumes of moisture into our area, resulting in 
widespread showers and thunderstorms likely for northern New 
York and southern Vermont. Northern Vermont is a little less 
certain, with several models keeping the main slug of rain from 
reaching the Vermont- Canada border and Northeast Kingdom, 
largely due to downsloping off the Green Mountains with a 
southeasterly flow. The main moisture and instability looks to 
be stationed over New York, with ridging anchored over Maine. 
Tuesday will also be one more chance for temperatures to reach 
the upper 70s and 80s before the system wicks away our warmth, 
which will help fuel any thunderstorms. Models are suggesting 
Pwats could reach as high as 1.75-2.00 inches in some locations,
and surface instability runs around 1500 J/kg, producing tall, 
skinny CAPE soundings. At times, storm motions look to run under
10 knots, indicating any showers or storms could be slow 
moving, heavy rainers. Forecast additional precipitation amounts
from early Tuesday morning into late Tuesday night will be as 
high as 0.50-1.00" Adirondacks and west as well as portions of 
southern Vermont. For the northern Champlain Valley as well as 
northern Vermont and southeastern Vermont, we're looking at 
closer to 0.05- 0.50". At the moment, the most likely 24 hour 
period for the St. Lawrence Valley to get 1 inch is Tuesday and 
Tuesday night. Any areas that see heavier downpours today will 
need to be especially watched on Tuesday. The WPC has a Marginal
(at least 5%) Risk of excessive rainfall over the entire 
forecast area Tuesday.

On Wednesday, the multi-layer low pressure swings southeast into the 
mid-Atlantic, continuing southeasterly to even easterly flow at 
times across the forecast area. Precipitation continues to look more 
likely in southern portions of the forecast area with downsloping in 
the wider valleys, and we lose the majority of instability. Our 
highs only reaching the upper 60s to mid 70s, we won't see the same 
convective showers and storms that we're expecting Tuesday. Still, 
steadier rain could produce as much as 0.75-1.25" of additional rain 
in southern Vermont, with 0.30-0.75" elsewhere. Wednesday is another 
period that the WPC has our entire area under Marginal Risk of 
excessive rainfall. River rises will be expected by Wednesday night 
following the bulk of the precipitation. At the moment, the most 
likely period of 1 inch within 24 hours for most of the area falls 
from Tuesday night to Wednesday, though southeastern Vermont could 
make out especially well Wednesday-Wednesday night in southeasterly 
flow. Once again, locations that receive heavy rain today or Tuesday 
will need to be closely monitored on Wednesday. Lingering showers 
and thunderstorms are also likely on Thursday as the upper level 
trough slowly exits the region and the occluded surface low remains 
nearby while temperatures rebound slightly into the 70s. Most likely 
location of any lingering showers or thunderstorms on Thursday will 
be eastern Vermont, closest to forcing.

KEY MESSAGE 3: An unsettled weather pattern continues for late week 
into next weekend as first system slowly departs by Friday, before 
another one arrives late Sat into Sunday. Still a large spread in 
timing of each system, especially toward next weekend, but cutoff 
and closed 7-5h circulation, feel the potential for showers wl 
linger into Friday associated with initial trof and weakening area 
of low pres. ECMWF shows weak differential heating boundary with 
some instability progged acrs northern NY/Champlain Valley, while 
deeper moisture/clouds linger over VT on Friday. This convergence 
and instability wl support a the threat for showers and embedded 
storms on Friday. 

Weak ridge tries to build into our cwa for Saturday, before next s/w 
and associated energy arrives late Saturday into Sunday. The 
evolution and track of 700-500mb trof, along with associated sfc low 
pres wl determine placement and areal coverage of showers/storms for 
this upcoming weekend. Latest guidances shows Saturday highest 
potential over northern NY, while Sunday activity wl be more 
widespread impacting both VT and NY. Limited run to run continuity 
and large spread in potential solutions results in low forecaster 
confidence and associated predictability on probability and timing 
of precip, especially Sunday into early next week. Temps wl be 
driven by clouds/precip, but mostly above normal values anticipated, 
especially at night with lows in the upper 50s to upper 60s, while 
highs range from the mid 70s to mid 80s. Some levels of humidity are 
expected, but the probability of much above normal temps or 
significant heat is low given anticipated pattern.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Through 12Z Tuesday...Any lingering fog and mist at SLK/MPV will
lift by 13 with VFR prevailing. A 20 to 30% probability of
showers with embedded storms are possible this afternoon, with
greatest potential over the northern TAF sites. Fog/mist will be
conditional on if any rain falls at a taf site this
aftn/evening. The highest potential will be at SLK, given
rainfall there yesterday. Light terrain driven winds will become
south-southwest at 4 to 8 knots by 15Z. 

Outlook...

Tuesday: VFR. Chance SHRA, Chance TSRA.
Tuesday Night: Mainly VFR, with local IFR possible. Chance SHRA,
Slight chance TSRA.
Wednesday: MVFR/IFR conditions possible. Definite SHRA, Chance
TSRA.
Wednesday Night: Mainly VFR, with local IFR possible. Chance
SHRA.
Thursday: MVFR/IFR conditions possible. Likely SHRA, Slight
chance TSRA.
Thursday Night: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Slight
chance SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Friday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Slight chance SHRA,
Slight chance TSRA.

&&
